901.text: A highlighted word is shown in bold type. Press and hold the mouse button on it to see what it means; let go and the explanation disappears.

910.text: The hard, light material that forms an insect's outer shell. It works as a skeleton on the outside of the body: it protects the ant and gives its muscles something to pull on.

911.text: A pair of small mouthparts just behind the jaws. They help to hold and chew food, and the ant also uses them to clean its legs and antennae.

912.text: Three tiny simple eyes on top of the head, found on some ants. They cannot make out shapes; they only tell light from dark.

913.text: A pouch under the mouth opening, also called the mouth pouch. Chewed food is squeezed here: the juice is swallowed and the dry leftovers are thrown away.

914.text: The ant's social stomach, a storage sac in the gaster. Food kept here is not for the ant itself but for sharing with its nestmates.

915.text: The ant's own stomach. The food that the ant keeps for itself is digested here and feeds its body.

916.text: Passing liquid food from mouth to mouth. Ants feed their nestmates in this way, so food is shared around the whole colony.

917.text: A group of ants with one body form and one kind of job, such as the queens, the workers or the soldiers.

918.text: The young that hatch from the eggs. A larva has no legs and no eyes; it is fed by the workers, does little but eat and grows quickly.

919.text: To change from a larva into a pupa. Many ant larvae do this by spinning a silk cocoon around themselves before they settle down to rest.

920.text: The main kinds of ant in a colony. Queens lay the eggs, workers dig, forage and nurse, soldiers defend the nest, and males mate.

921.text: The resting stage between larva and adult. Inside the cocoon, the young ant's body is rebuilt into the body of an adult.

922.text: To come out of the pupal case or cocoon as an adult. In many species the workers help by tearing the cocoon open.

923.text: Young adult ants that have just emerged. They are soft and pale at first, and within a few days they darken and harden.

924.text: Chemical messages. An ant gives off a pheromone and other ants of its species can sense it, for example to follow a trail, to give an alarm or to recognise nestmates.

925.text: The young of the colony: the eggs, the larvae and the pupae. The workers feed them, clean them and carry them from room to room.

926.text: The sugary liquid that aphids give off after drinking plant sap. Many ants love it and collect it as food.

927.text: Small, soft insects that suck the sap of plants. Some ants guard them and collect the honeydew they produce.

928.text: The game's word for the winged males and the new queens. They fly off to mate and then start new colonies.

929.text: To get nestmates to help with a job, using scent signals and touch.

963.text: To go out and look for food, and to collect it and bring it back to the nest.

964.text: The search for food outside the nest and the work of carrying it home. The ants that do this job are called foragers.

965.text: The room of the nest where the queen lives and lays her eggs. Workers feed her there and keep her clean.

966.text: The rooms where the eggs, larvae and pupae are kept. Nurse workers feed the young there and move them from chamber to chamber as needed.

967.text: The first stage of an ant's life. It is small and hatches after some weeks. A fertilised egg grows into a female ant; an egg that was not fertilised becomes a male.
